passages.original: II. Contra obiectionem Pelagii, qua dicit paruulos baptismo non egere.
passages.english: II. Against the objection of Pelagius, in which he says that infants do not need baptism.

passages.original: Dicit ergo Pelagius, quod ad obtinendam salutem natura hominis sibi sola sufficiat. ita haec pestifer doctor adfirmat, quasi adhuc factura conditionis nostrae in statu suo inlibata permaneat. ego arbitror, quod libertas arbitrii sibi sola sufficere sine praesidio gratiae non potuerit, etiam antequam priuilegium illius transgressio prima uiolaret.
passages.english: Pelagius, then, says that for obtaining salvation human nature by itself is sufficient for itself. This pestilent teacher asserts these things as though the making of our created state still remained unimpaired in its condition. I judge that freedom of choice could not have been sufficient for itself alone without the protection of grace, even before the first transgression violated its privilege.

passages.original: Asserit ergo Pelagius Adam, siue peccasset siue non peccasset, omnimodis fuisse moriturum. et hoc ex ipsa prauitate descendit, qua negat originale delictum. dum enim adfirmare contendit mort[al]em necessitatem conditionis fuisse, non transgressionis, uult uideri originem huius debiti non a seruo, sed a domino, non a contemptore, sed ab auctore coepisse, ut mortis lex ordinationis credatur esse, non criminis.
passages.english: Pelagius, then, asserts that Adam, whether he had sinned or had not sinned, would in every case have died. And this comes down from that very depravity by which he denies original sin. For while he strives to affirm that death was a necessity of [our] created state, not of transgression, he wishes it to appear that the origin of this debt began not from the servant but from the Lord, not from the one who showed contempt but from the Author, so that the law of death may be believed to belong to [God's] ordering, not to crime.
passages.notes: The edition prints 'mort[al]em'; read as 'mortem' (death), the bracketed letters apparently marked for deletion.

passages.original: II. CONTRA OBIECTIONEM PELAGII, QVA DICIT PAEUULOS BAPTISMO NON EGERE.
passages.english: II. Against the objection of Pelagius, in which he says that infants do not need baptism.

passages.original: Sed dicit Pelagius ideo non esse originale peccatum, quia ipsa concupiscentia generationis ex deo sit. unde autem ueniat nexus iste, qui posteros trahit, si requiras: sine dubio per incentiuum maledictae generationis ardorem et per inlecebrosum utriusque parentis amplexum.
passages.english: But Pelagius says that there is therefore no original sin, because the very concupiscence of generation is from God. Yet if you ask whence comes this bond that draws [our] descendants along: without doubt through the inciting heat of accursed generation and through the seductive embrace of both parents.

passages.original: sed inmaculatos thoros caro maledictioni addicta maculauit et per superbiae spiritum simplicem corrupit affectum et sicut inmortalitatis priuilegium, ita donum perdidit puritatis. non in querellam uocatur nuptialis gratia, sed obscenae passionis iniuria. non aurum in culpam uenit, sed quidquid auro obryzo adulterinum fraus iniquitatis admiscuit, sicut ipsius Pelagii spiritum ad meliora studia a deo conditum corruptione pestifera nequitiae auctor infecit.
passages.english: But the flesh, consigned to the curse, defiled the unstained marriage bed, and through the spirit of pride corrupted [its] simple affection, and just as it lost the privilege of immortality, so [it lost] the gift of purity. It is not the grace of marriage that is called into complaint, but the injury of obscene passion. It is not the gold that comes under blame, but whatever adulterate matter the fraud of iniquity has mixed into the refined gold, just as the author of wickedness infected, with pestilent corruption, the spirit of Pelagius himself, which was created by God for better pursuits.

passages.original: sed quia fatalis persuasio, quae uim praescientiae cogentis inducit, omnimodis respuenda est, ideo magis et legem (deus) dedit et prophetas mediis temporibus excitauit, quia arbitrium uoluntatis humanae adtenuatum nouerat, non ablatum. quod si ex toto uigor eius perisset, quomodo legeretur: et in lege domini fuit uoluntas eius, et iterum: uoluntarie sacrificabo tibi, domine, et ad Philemonem: ut non ex necessitate, sed uoluntarium esset bonum tuum? et cum dicat in euangelio: caro mea est, quam ego dabo pro mundi uita, dubitare penitus non debemus, quod pro toto mundo se inpenderit, qui plus dedit, quam totus mundus ualebat, sicut et beatus Iohannes euangelista testatur: ipse est enim propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, sed et pro totius mundi.
passages.english: But since the fatalistic doctrine, which brings in the force of a compelling foreknowledge, must be rejected in every way, for that reason all the more did (God) give the law and raise up prophets in the intervening times, because he knew that the choice of the human will had been weakened, not taken away. But if its vigour had perished entirely, how would one read: "and his will was in the law of the Lord," and again: "I will sacrifice to you willingly, O Lord," and to Philemon: "so that your good might not be of necessity but voluntary"? And since he says in the Gospel: "it is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world," we ought not to doubt at all that he spent himself for the whole world, he who gave more than the whole world was worth, just as the blessed John the Evangelist also testifies: "for he is the propitiation for our sins, and also for [those] of the whole world."
passages.notes: '(deus)' is an editorial supplement in the edition.

passages.original: Opus itaque naturalis legis in cordibus hominum fuisse conscriptum etiam beatissimus pontifex Augustinus doctissimo sermone prosequitur ita dicens: utrumque simul currit in isto alueo atque torrente generis humani, malum, quod a parente trahitur, et bonum, quod a creante tribuitur. item nullius quippe uitium ita contra naturam est, ut naturae deleat etiam extrema uestigia. nam hinc est, quod etiam impii cogitant aeterna ac praedicanda etiam in praesenti saeculo iura constituunt et multa recte reprehendunt recteque laudant in hominum moribus.
passages.english: Accordingly, that the work of the natural law was written in the hearts of men the most blessed bishop Augustine also sets out in a most learned discourse, saying thus: "Both run together in this channel and torrent of the human race: the evil which is drawn from the parent, and the good which is bestowed by the Creator." Likewise: "For no one's vice is so contrary to nature that it blots out even the last traces of nature. For hence it is that even the ungodly think of eternal things, and even in the present age establish laws worthy to be proclaimed, and rightly censure many things and rightly praise [many] in the conduct of men."
passages.notes: The work is the De gratia of Faustus of Riez, quoting Augustine. The quotations are given as the text presents them, with no attempt to check them against Augustine's own wording. The phrase "aeterna ac praedicanda etiam in praesenti saeculo iura" is awkward as transmitted. It might instead be read as "establish eternal laws, worthy to be proclaimed even in the present age". Here "aeterna" has been taken as the object of "cogitant".
